subject: mathematics_2a
question_text: If cos α + cos β + cos γ = 0 = sin α + sin β + sin γ, then show that (i) cos 3α + cos 3β + cos 3γ = 3cos(α + β + γ), (ii) sin 3α + sin 3β + sin 3γ = 3 sin(α + β + γ), (iii) cos(α + β) + cos(β + γ) + cos(γ + α) = 0.

mark_split.label: Let a = cis α, b = cis β, c = cis γ; a + b + c = 0
a + b + c = 0 ⇒ a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc
De Moivre and the product rule
Results (i) and (ii) from real and imaginary parts

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove the three results — what you call a, b, c, which identity gives the cubes, how De Moivre gives the triple angles, and where the third result comes from.
insider_note: Results (i) and (ii) are one equation read twice. Result (iii) needs a second idea, the reciprocals, and is where the last two marks are decided.

steps.label: Let a = cis α, b = cis β, c = cis γ
steps.margin_note: First mark. Put a = cis α, b = cis β, c = cis γ; the two given sums are the real and imaginary parts of a + b + c, so a + b + c = 0 + i(0) = 0. Show both parts — writing a + b + c = 0 straight away skips what earns the mark.
lines: Let a = cos α + i sin α = cis α,
b = cis β, c = cis γ. Then
a + b + c = (cos α + cos β + cos γ)
+ i(sin α + sin β + sin γ) = 0 + i(0) = 0

recall.must_convey: That a = cis α, b = cis β, c = cis γ are introduced and the two given sums make a + b + c = 0 + i(0) = 0.
accept: let a b c be cis alpha cis beta cis gamma then a plus b plus c is zero from the given sums
the sum of the cosines and the sum of the sines are both zero so a plus b plus c equals zero
put a equals cis alpha and so on and add them, real and imaginary parts are both zero
a b c ni cis alpha beta gamma ga teeskunte a plus b plus c zero avuthundi
combine the two given equations into one complex equation a plus b plus c equals zero

steps.why: Three real equations become one complex equation a + b + c = 0. Everything after this is algebra on a, b, c; the trigonometry comes back only at the end when real and imaginary parts are separated.
common_mistakes: Writing a + b + c = 0 without showing that both the real part and the imaginary part are given to be zero.
Using cis α to mean cos α − i sin α.
Naming a, b, c and never using the given condition.

steps.label: a + b + c = 0 ⇒ a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Because a + b + c = 0, the identity a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca) leaves a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc. Keep the 3; it is the 3 on the right of results (i) and (ii).
lines: a + b + c = 0 ⇒ a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc

recall.must_convey: That a + b + c = 0 implies a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc, and this is written with a, b, c as cis α, cis β, cis γ.
accept: when a plus b plus c is zero, a cubed plus b cubed plus c cubed equals three a b c
use the identity a cubed plus b cubed plus c cubed minus three a b c equals a plus b plus c times something, so the cubes sum to three a b c
the cube identity gives a cubed plus b cubed plus c cubed is three a b c
a plus b plus c zero aithe cubes sum three abc avuthundi
write cis alpha cubed plus cis beta cubed plus cis gamma cubed equals three times the product

steps.why: a³ + b³ + c³ − 3abc = (a + b + c)(a² + b² + c² − ab − bc − ca), so a + b + c = 0 gives a³ + b³ + c³ = 3abc. This is the identity that produces the 3 and the triple angles in results (i) and (ii).
common_mistakes: Cubing a + b + c = 0 by expanding, instead of using the standard identity.

steps.label: De Moivre: cis 3α + cis 3β + cis 3γ = 3 cis(α + β + γ)
steps.margin_note: Third mark. De Moivre gives (cis α)³ = cis 3α, and the product rule gives (cis α)(cis β)(cis γ) = cis(α + β + γ). Angles add in a product of cis numbers; they are never multiplied.
lines: ⇒ cis 3α + cis 3β + cis 3γ = 3 cis(α + β + γ)
= 3cos(α + β + γ) + i · 3 sin(α + β + γ)

recall.must_convey: That by De Moivre (cis α)³ = cis 3α and the product cis α · cis β · cis γ = cis(α + β + γ), then both sides are split into real and imaginary parts.
accept: cis alpha cubed is cis three alpha by De Moivre and the product is cis of alpha plus beta plus gamma, then split into real and imaginary parts
the cubes give triple angles and the product adds the angles
write cos three alpha plus cos three beta plus cos three gamma plus i times the sines equals three cis alpha plus beta plus gamma
De Moivre tho cis three alpha, product lo angles add avuthai, real imaginary parts separate cheyyali
left side is triple angles, right side is three cis of the sum of the angles

steps.why: De Moivre's theorem turns the cubes into triple angles and the product rule turns abc into cis of the sum. Writing both sides as real part plus i times imaginary part is what allows the two results to be read off.
common_mistakes: Writing (cis α)³ = cos³ α + i sin³ α.
Multiplying the angles in abc instead of adding them.
Forgetting the 3 on the right-hand side.

steps.label: Results (i) and (ii)
steps.margin_note: Fourth and fifth marks. Two complex numbers are equal only when both parts agree, so this one line gives (i) from the real parts and (ii) from the imaginary parts. The right side is 3cos(α + β + γ), not cos 3(α + β + γ).
lines: sin 3α + sin 3β + sin 3γ = 3 sin(α + β + γ)

recall.must_convey: That equating real parts gives result (i) and equating imaginary parts gives result (ii).
accept: equate the real parts for the cosine result and the imaginary parts for the sine result
real parts give cos three alpha plus cos three beta plus cos three gamma equals three cos of the sum, imaginary parts give the sine version
results one and two are the real and imaginary parts of the same equation
real parts equate cheste one, imaginary parts equate cheste two vasthundi
compare the real parts and then the imaginary parts

steps.why: Two complex numbers are equal only when their real parts agree and their imaginary parts agree. One complex equation therefore carries both results, which is why they share two marks.
common_mistakes: Proving (i) and stopping, forgetting that (ii) is the imaginary part of the same line.
Writing the right-hand side as cos 3(α + β + γ).

steps.label: Result (iii)
steps.margin_note: Sixth and seventh marks. 1/a = cis(−α), so 1/a + 1/b + 1/c is the same given data with the sine sign reversed, and it is 0. Multiply through by abc to get ab + bc + ca = 0; each product is cis of a sum of two angles, and the real parts give result (iii).
lines: − i(sin α + sin β + sin γ) = 0 − i(0) = 0
⇒ cis(α + β) + cis(β + γ) + cis(γ + α) = 0

lines.text: cos(α + β) + cos(β + γ) + cos(γ + α) = 0

recall.must_convey: That 1/a + 1/b + 1/c = 0 (the reciprocals are cis(−α) etc.), so ab + bc + ca = 0, which is cis(α + β) + cis(β + γ) + cis(γ + α) = 0, and its real part is result (iii).
accept: the reciprocals are cis minus alpha and so on and their sum is zero, so a b plus b c plus c a is zero, which gives cis alpha plus beta plus cis beta plus gamma plus cis gamma plus alpha zero, real parts give three
one by a plus one by b plus one by c is zero so a b plus b c plus c a is zero and equating real parts proves the third
the sum of the reciprocals is zero, multiply by a b c, then take real parts
reciprocal sum zero, so ab plus bc plus ca zero, real parts teeste cos alpha plus beta sum zero
a b is cis alpha plus beta and the three such terms add to zero
heard_as: a b plus b c plus c a

steps.why: The reciprocals are the conjugates, so the given condition also makes their sum zero. Clearing the denominator turns that into ab + bc + ca = 0, and each product is cis of a sum of two angles — exactly the angles in result (iii).
common_mistakes: Writing 1/a = cis α with no sign change.
Forgetting to multiply through by abc, and trying to read (iii) off the reciprocal sum directly.
Writing ab = cis(αβ) instead of cis(α + β).
